# The Old Country of Night

Night used to be a country with its own laws, its own economy, its own citizens. When the sun went down, the world did not simply dim — it changed governments. Doors were barred, fires banked, voices lowered, and a different set of rules took over: rules about who could move through the dark, what could be said aloud, which hours belonged to which activities. Even our word *curfew* remembers this — from the old French *couvre-feu*, "cover the fire," the bell that told a town to extinguish its flames and submit to darkness. We tend to imagine pre-industrial nights as our nights minus electricity. They weren't. They were another civilization running in parallel with the daylight one, and almost everything we know about how it felt has been forgotten within living memory of the grid.

Consider what darkness actually meant indoors. Candles were luxury goods. Tallow — rendered animal fat — smoked, guttered, and smelled like a slaughterhouse. Beeswax burned clean but cost dearly. A working family often made do with rushlights: dried rushes soaked in kitchen grease, clamped upright in a holder, each one sputtering out a weak cone of light for mere minutes. Light had a price per hour the way bread had a price per loaf, and most people simply couldn't afford to be awake. Outdoors, the moon served as public infrastructure. Full-moon nights were for travel and late harvests; the black of the moon belonged to whoever had business best done unseen.

And sleep — this is the strangest part — came in two installments. The historian Roger Ekirch, combing centuries of diaries, court records, medical texts, and letters, documented it over and over: "first sleep," then a natural waking around midnight lasting an hour or two, then "second sleep" until dawn. The interval had its own names — *the watch* in England, *dorveille* in France, a word that hovers beautifully between sleep and waking. People didn't lie awake worrying. They got up. They prayed, tended embers, talked in low voices, made love, brewed beer, occasionally slipped next door to visit a neighbor, or simply lay thinking while the house breathed around them. Among the Tiv people of West Africa, the two sleeps were named independently of any European influence — evidence not of local eccentricity but of something closer to a species-wide default.

In the 1990s, the researcher Thomas Wehr effectively rebuilt the old night in a laboratory. Volunteers given fourteen hours of darkness — a reasonable approximation of a winter night before electricity — split their sleep cleanly in two: a long first stretch, a calm interlude of quiet wakefulness accompanied by a distinctive hormonal shift, then a second stretch. Given enough darkness, the biphasic night reasserted itself, as if it had been waiting in the body all along.

Then came the light. Gas lamps, kerosene, and finally the filament and the grid pushed the dark back street by street, decade by decade. As the usable evening lengthened, the two sleeps fused into one. The midnight interval shrank from a shared institution to a private embarrassment. Today, waking at three in the morning gets filed under *insomnia* — a malfunction, something to medicate — when for thousands of years it was simply what human bodies did, an inherited appointment kept quietly in the dark.

None of this is an argument for romanticizing the dark. The old night was genuinely dangerous — cold, fire, illness, violence — and it locked most people out of knowledge after sundown; no laborer could learn to read by a rushlight that cost more than his supper. Electric light gave us night shifts and emergency surgery and children reading under blankets past bedtime. Nobody sane would hand that back.

But notice what was traded away. Go far from any city on a clear night and look up until you find the faint pale river arched overhead: the Milky Way, our own galaxy seen edge-on from within. For every human being who lived before the last few generations, that band was as ordinary as weather — visible from every village, every desert, every ship, every doorway. A recent global atlas of light pollution estimated that a third of humanity can no longer see it at all, including the large majority of people in Europe and North America. Sit with that for a moment. The single oldest shared experience of our species — the one spectacle every ancestor, everywhere, stood beneath on clear nights — has been erased for most people alive today. Not by war or catastrophe. By porch lights.

Something subtler went, too: a texture of consciousness. Waking in the middle of the night meant surfacing *inside* a dream, carrying its logic into the firelit hour of the watch, where it mingled with prayer and worry and plan-making. People wrote their dreams down because they woke holding pieces of them. The seam between sleeping and waking — where a great deal of the old world's religion, storytelling, and self-examination lived — has been sewn shut. Our consolidated sleep is more efficient now. Efficiency does that sort of thing.

There is a remedy, and it is cheap and entirely legal: go find real darkness. Once a year, if you can manage it, wait for a moonless night and drive past the glow of towns until the sky stops being orange at the horizon. Lie back on something warm and give your eyes half an hour — the full adaptation takes longer than anyone expects, which is why most people have never seen their own night vision at full power. Then watch the smear of the galaxy resolve into structure, into dark rifts and dense light, ten thousand suns' worth of distance flattened into milk. Your retinas will be doing precisely what a Roman shepherd's did, what a Song dynasty poet's did, what a fur trader's did on the same date in a different millennium. Very few human experiences travel across time untouched. This is the grandest of them, and the ticket costs nothing but gasoline and a little discomfort.

Because the night never actually left. We just stopped visiting. It waits beyond the last streetlight with its old laws intact — the watch, the dream, the wheeling river overhead. And somewhere in your body, deeper than habit, the second sleep keeps its appointment still, patient as anything ancient, waiting only for the lights to go out long enough — once — to keep it.

Let me think about what would be genuinely interesting to write. Free writing is an invitation to be authentic and thoughtful. What might be compelling?

Options:
1. An essay on some intellectual topic — memory, time, language, attention

I think a reflective essay that's genuinely interesting would work well. Let me pick a topic I can explore with depth: perhaps the nature of maps and territories, or the history of a small thing (like the color blue, or lighthouses), or something about night, or about the strange fact that we can never step in the same river twice.

Let me consider what would show genuine craft. An essay braiding together several observations around a single theme could be beautiful. Theme candidates:
- Waiting / patience
- Margins (of pages, of cities, of maps)
- The color of things before photography
- Sound that has vanished forever
- The future that never arrived
- Light — starlight being old news; every star we see is the past

I like the theme of light/time — but it's common. What about "the archaeology of ordinary moments"? Or an essay on doors? Doors are wonderful: thresholds, privacy, the invention of the hinge, "knock knock," liminality. Hmm.

What about writing about the night — specifically, how pre-industrial people experienced night differently: segmented sleep ("first sleep" and "second sleep" documented by historian Roger Ekirch), the moon as the only streetlight, fear and community. **The Old Country of Night**

Night used to be a country with its own laws, its own economy, its own citizens. When the sun went down, the world did not dim so much as change governments. Doors were barred, fires banked, conversations dropped to murmurs, and a different set of rules took over — rules about who could move through the dark, what could be said aloud, which hours belonged to which activities. We tend to imagine that pre-industrial nights were simply our nights minus electricity. They weren't. They were another civilization, running in parallel with the daylight one, and most of what we know about how it felt has been forgotten within living memory of the grid.

(~110 words)

Consider what darkness meant indoors... candles were luxury items. Tallow — rendered animal fat — smoked, guttered, smelled like a slaughterhouse. Beeswax burned clean but cost... A working family often made do with rushlights: dried rushes soaked in kitchen grease, pinned upright in a holder, each giving off a weak sputter of light for minutes at a time. Light had a price per hour the way bread had a price per loaf... The moon was public infrastructure. Full-moon nights were for travel, markets, harvests pushed late; the dark of the moon belonged to those with business best done unseen.

(~120)

And sleep — this is the strangest part. For most of human history, sleep came in two installments. Historian Roger Ekirch, combing through diaries, court records, medical texts, letters spanning centuries and continents, documented it again and again: "first sleep," then a natural waking around midnight lasting an hour or two, then "second sleep" until dawn. The interval had names — the watch, the dread... People didn't lie awake anxious. They got up. They prayed... talked by ember-light, had sex, visited neighbors, brewed beer, or simply lay thinking while the house breathed around them. In parts of West Africa, the Tiv people named the two sleeps independently, proof this wasn't European eccentricity but something closer to a species-wide default.

(~130)

In the 1990s, a researcher named Thomas Wehr put volunteers in fourteen hours of darkness — approximating a winter's night — and watched their sleep split neatly down the middle: a first stretch, a calm interlude of quiet wakefulness marked by a hormonal shift, then a second stretch. Given enough dark, the two-part night reasserted itself, as if it had been waiting in the body all along.

(~75)

Then came the light. Gas lamps, kerosene, and finally the filament and the grid, pushing back the dark street by street, decade by decade. As evening lengthened, the two sleeps fused into one. The midnight interval shrank from a shared institution to a private embarrassment. Today, waking at three in the morning is filed under insomnia — a malfunction, something to fix — when for thousands of years it was simply what human bodies did, an inherited appointment kept quietly in the dark.

(~85)

None of this is an argument for romanticizing the dark... The old night was dangerous... disease, fire, cold, violence... darkness excluded people from knowledge after sundown; illiterate laborers couldn't study by a rushlight that cost more than their dinner. Electric light gave us night shifts and emergency surgery and children reading past bedtime. Nobody sane would give that back.

(~70)

But notice what got traded away. Look up on a clear night, far from a city — really far — and find the faint pale river overhead: the Milky Way, our own galaxy seen edge-on from inside. For every human who ever lived before the last few generations, that band was as ordinary as weather... A recent global atlas of light pollution estimated that a third of humanity can no longer see it at all, including most people in Europe and North America. This is worth sitting with: the single oldest shared experience of our species — the one spectacle every ancestor, everywhere, stood beneath on clear nights — has been erased for most of the people alive today. Not by catastrophe. By porch lights.

(~130)

Something subtler went too: a texture of consciousness... Waking in the middle of the night meant surfacing inside a dream... People wrote their dreams down because they woke holding pieces of them... The seam between sleeping and waking, where much of the old world's religion, storytelling, and self-examination lived, has been sewn shut. Our sleep is more efficient now. Efficiency does that kind of thing.

(~80)

There's a remedy, cheap and legal: go find real darkness. Once a year if you can manage it, on a moonless night, drive past the glow of towns until the sky stops being orange... Then lie back and look up until your eyes adjust fully — it takes half an hour... The smear of the galaxy will resolve... Your retinas will be doing precisely what a Roman shepherd's did, what a Song dynasty poet's did... Some experiences travel across millennia untouched; this is the greatest of them, and the ticket costs nothing but gasoline and a little discomfort.

(~115)

Because the night itself never left. We stopped visiting... It still holds its old laws somewhere beyond the last streetlight... And somewhere in your body, deeper than habit, the second sleep keeps its appointment — waiting for the lights to go out long enough, once, for it to keep them.
